newsitem.title: USA: Gene shown to repair spinal cord injuries in rats.
newsitem.headline: Gene shown to repair spinal cord injuries in rats.

text.p: Researchers said on Monday they reversed paralysis in laboratory rats using a gene therapy they hope could eventually be used to repair human spinal cord injuries.

Although such a potential treatment is a long way from being perfected, doctors said it offered new promise for a currently untreatable condition. Some 200,000 Americans are partly or completely paralysed because of spinal injuries, most frequently caused by automobile or diving accidents.
Researchers at the University of California at San Diego tested the treatment in laboratory rats. Their spinal cords were damaged in a way that impaired their ability to walk.

The gene therapy involved removing some of the rats' healthy cells, infusing them with a gene that stimulates the production of a growth factor, and then transplanting those genetically altered cells into the site of the spinal cord injury.
After three months, the researchers measured the improvement by observing the rats walk across a test grid.

The rats which had been treated with the gene therapy made two to three errors during the test, compared with an average of about eight made by the injured rats in the control group. Completely healthy rats made an average of less than one error while walking the test grid.
The lead investigator in the study, Dr. Mark Tuszynski, associate professor of neurosciences at the UCSD School of Medicine, published the results in the July 15 issue of the Journal of Neuroscience.

"The report shows there is hope for generating some recovery of function after a spinal cord injury," Tuszynski said, adding that it could offer benefits over another experimental treatment involving transplanting spinal tissue from aborted foetuses.

"The cells you would use in gene therapy would be a person's own cells," he said. "They are essentially available with a limitless supply. They are available immediately, and there is no ethical controversy associated with it."
Doctors have recently begun testing foetal tissue transplants in paralysed patients to see if this could stimulate the damaged tissue to rebuild itself.
Tuszynski said he hoped to obtain federal funding to continue to test the gene therapy on larger animals that are anatomically closer to humans.
